title: Best Weekly Planner Apps (2026): 5 Tools Compared
summary: Compare the best weekly planner apps for 2026, including Akiflow, Sunsama, Motion, Todoist and Tweek, with prices, planning styles and clear limits.
body_markdown:
**Summary**


-


Akiflow is the best overall weekly planner for professionals who want one loop from task intake and goals to calendar time and review.


-


Sunsama emphasizes objectives, Motion automates placement, Todoist remains task-first, and Tweek keeps the week visually simple.


-


Test one normal week plus a midweek disruption to see whether the app reveals lost capacity and gives unfinished work a clear next destination.


## What are the best weekly planner apps in 2026?


The best weekly planner apps in 2026 are Akiflow, Sunsama, Motion, Todoist, and Tweek. Akiflow is our overall recommendation because its documented weekly ritual, broader time frames, task intake, and calendar time blocking cover the full planning loop. The other products are better choices for objective-led, automatic, task-first, or minimalist planning.


A weekly planner should do more than display seven columns. It needs a way to collect commitments, choose outcomes, see calendar capacity, place important work, recover unfinished tasks, and close the week with enough context to plan the next one. Apps differ sharply in which of those decisions they guide, automate, or leave to the user.


We reviewed current official feature, help, and pricing information on August 24, 2026. This is a researched comparison, not a claim of hands-on testing. Evaluation covers weekly review, goals or objectives, calendar planning, automation, carry-forward behavior, documented integrations, and plan cost. The[weekly review method](https://akiflow.com/blog/weekly-review-method-tasks) explains the underlying planning habit.


The main choice is control. Akiflow uses structured rituals but leaves calendar placement to the planner. Sunsama separates broad weekly objectives from detailed daily scheduling. Motion automatically places tasks around fixed events. Todoist supplies task organization without a dedicated weekly ritual in the source reviewed. Tweek recreates a simple paper-like week with manual control.


Weekly planning also needs a clear boundary between commitments and possibilities. A planner that places every backlog item into the next seven days creates false precision; one that shows only appointments hides the work competing for the remaining hours. The strongest products help users identify a small set of outcomes, inspect fixed calendar demand, and decide which flexible tasks deserve capacity. The comparison therefore rewards tools that make overload visible and give displaced work an understandable destination. It does not reward an app merely for displaying a week or offering many decorative views.


### Weekly planner apps compared


1.


**Akiflow**


-


**Best for:** A complete weekly execution loop


-


**Weekly model:** Ritual, time frames, and time blocking


-


**Price:** $34 monthly or $19/mo billed yearly


-


**Main tradeoff:** Paid and manually directed


2.


**Sunsama**


-


**Best for:** Weekly objectives and reflection


-


**Weekly model:** Objectives weekly, detailed scheduling daily


-


**Price:** $22 monthly or $204 yearly


-


**Main tradeoff:** Does not schedule every task in the weekly ritual


3.


**Motion**


-


**Best for:** Automatic weekly scheduling


-


**Weekly model:** Algorithm places tasks around fixed events


-


**Price:** $19/seat/mo billed yearly


-


**Main tradeoff:** Algorithm controls task placement


4.


**Todoist**


-


**Best for:** A lightweight task-first week


-


**Weekly model:** Projects, filters, deadlines, and Pro calendar


-


**Price:** Free; Pro $60/year


-


**Main tradeoff:** No dedicated weekly ritual documented


5.


**Tweek**


-


**Best for:** A paper-like visual week


-


**Weekly model:** Manual board with notes and colors


-


**Price:** Free; Premium $49.99/year


-


**Main tradeoff:** Limited integrations and no automatic scheduling


## 1. Akiflow


Choose Akiflow if weekly planning must connect incoming tasks, goals, calendar capacity, and daily execution. Its weekly planning ritual reviews completed and overdue work, prior goals, new weekly goals and notes, broader time frames, time slots, and time blocking. That makes it the most complete documented weekly loop in this comparison.


The Upcoming page extends the planning horizon with Overview, Days, Weeks, and Months views plus time frames for This Week, Next Week, This Month, Next Month, and Someday. A task can remain in a broader time frame until the planner is ready to place it on a day or into a calendar slot. The[weekly work plan guide](https://akiflow.com/blog/create-weekly-work-plan) shows how those decisions fit together.


The Akiflow Pro plan lists $34 monthly and $19 per month on annual billing; a 7-day trial is available. It includes tasks, subtasks, meetings, integrations, quick capture, daily planning, recurring tasks, priorities, time blocking, availability sharing, calendar sync, desktop and mobile apps, and productivity analytics. Weekly planning is part of the same product used for daily execution.


The tradeoff is a paid, hands-on planning model. The official pricing reviewed lists a trial and paid Pro plan rather than a permanent free tier, and unexpected calendar changes still require the user to make planning decisions. Choose Motion when automatic rescheduling is the priority. Choose Akiflow when reviewing and placing the week personally is a feature, not unwanted labor. Our[best daily planner apps](https://akiflow.com/blog/daily-planner-time-slots) comparison narrows the day-level decision.


The broader time-frame model is important because not every useful task is ready for a date. Work can remain associated with this week or a later planning horizon until the weekly review has enough context to schedule it. That prevents the calendar from becoming a collection of speculative promises. Once a task becomes a real commitment, it can move into a day or time block beside meetings. This separation between horizon, day, and calendar slot gives the planner several levels of commitment without requiring duplicate tasks or an external holding list.


## 2. Sunsama


Choose Sunsama if the purpose of weekly planning is to define a small set of objectives and reflect on progress without scheduling every task upfront. Its weekly ritual can carry objectives forward, add a reflection, combine review and planning, retain prior weekly plans, and share the resulting plan to Slack or Teams.


Sunsama explicitly recommends planning weekly objectives rather than every task, leaving detailed scheduling to daily planning. That separation is useful for managers or professionals who want a strategic weekly frame without pretending every hour can be decided in advance. It also means the app expects an ongoing daily routine to translate objectives into specific calendar commitments.


Sunsama costs $22 per user monthly or $204 yearly, equivalent to $17 per month, with a 14-day trial and one paid product tier. The official[Sunsama weekly planning guide](https://help.sunsama.com/docs/usage-guides/weekly-objectives/weekly-planning/) explains the ritual, while the billing page confirms the current plan structure.


The tradeoff is deliberate scope: the weekly ritual does not attempt to schedule every task. Choose Sunsama when objectives and reflection are the missing discipline. Choose Akiflow when the same weekly process also needs broader time frames and calendar time blocking, or Motion when the primary requirement is automatic placement rather than a guided review.


Sunsama's objective layer is most useful when the week needs direction before it needs detail. A product launch, hiring decision, or client milestone can remain visible as a weekly outcome while its specific actions are chosen during daily planning. That keeps the weekly review from becoming an attempt to predict every interruption. The approach depends on returning to the daily ritual; objectives alone do not reserve time. Buyers should test whether that two-level rhythm feels clarifying or whether they would rather place important work into the calendar during the weekly session itself.


## 3. Motion


Choose Motion if you want the weekly schedule to be assembled automatically from task priorities, durations, deadlines, availability, and fixed calendar events. Motion Pro AI is the most automation-led option here. It suits people who are comfortable letting software decide where tasks belong as the available week changes.


The working model is input-driven: tasks need enough timing and priority information for the scheduler to place them. Motion then fills open calendar capacity around meetings and other fixed commitments. When conditions change, the algorithm can place pending work again. That removes some manual placement while also giving the algorithm more influence over sequence and timing.


Motion Pro AI costs $19 per seat per month billed yearly. That tier combines AI projects and tasks, calendar and meetings, docs and notes, an AI task planner, integrations, and desktop and mobile apps. Check the current[Motion pricing page](https://www.usemotion.com/pricing) before purchase because the lowest quoted monthly rate depends on annual billing.


The tradeoff is control over placement. A person who cares deeply about doing specific work at a particular hour may spend time overriding an automatically generated plan. Motion is a strong choice when frequent calendar change makes manual rescheduling the larger burden. It is a weaker fit when the planning review itself is how priorities are clarified.


Automation is valuable when the week contains enough change that manual placement becomes repetitive. It is less valuable when priorities depend on context the task record does not capture, such as waiting for a stakeholder, protecting a creative sequence, or choosing work based on energy. A representative trial should include those ambiguous cases rather than only clean deadline-driven tasks. If the generated calendar repeatedly needs human correction, the buyer may prefer a manual planner with faster rescheduling. If the placements remain sensible after changes, Motion can remove a substantial amount of weekly maintenance.


## 4. Todoist


Choose Todoist if the week can be managed through projects, deadlines, filters, reminders, and a task-first review. Beginner is free and includes quick capture, reminders, list and board layouts, filters, and integrations. Pro adds calendar layout, task duration, custom reminders, deadlines, Task Assist, and full reporting history.


A weekly routine in Todoist can begin by reviewing projects and overdue work, using filters to isolate the next set of commitments, and adding deadlines or durations where they matter. Pro's calendar layout can show those tasks in time. The source material reviewed does not document a dedicated weekly objectives-and-shutdown ritual comparable to Akiflow or Sunsama.


Annual billing makes Todoist Pro $60 per year, equivalent to $5 per month; paying month to month costs $7. The free Beginner plan makes it practical to test the lighter task model, but calendar layout and task duration require Pro. Verify currency and taxes on the[Todoist pricing page](https://www.todoist.com/pricing) .


Todoist is the right choice when a dependable task system is more important than a prescribed weekly process. It leaves more of the review method to the user, which can be freedom or a missing layer depending on planning habits. Add a separate ritual only if the team or individual will actually maintain it every week.


Todoist can support a disciplined weekly review even though it does not prescribe one in the same way as the ritual-led products. The user can review each active project, clear overdue items, inspect upcoming deadlines, and apply labels or filters for the coming week. That flexibility is attractive to people who already trust their method. It is less helpful to someone buying software specifically because the review never happens. The product provides capable task organization; the planner must supply the cadence, capacity check, and rules for deciding what does not enter the week.


## 5. Tweek


Choose Tweek if a weekly planner should look and behave more like a paper week than a project-management system. Its low-friction weekly board emphasizes visual simplicity, color coding, recurring tasks, notes, reminders, sharing, templates, and web and mobile access. It is the clearest minimalist option in this comparison.


The workflow is intentionally manual: place commitments on the weekly board, use colors or notes to distinguish them, and carry the plan across web and mobile. That makes the week easy to scan without asking an algorithm to interpret priorities. It also avoids the intake and configuration layers that define the more elaborate products in this guide.


Tweek's free plan can be used indefinitely. Premium costs $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year and includes a 14-day trial; it adds Google and Apple calendar sync, subtasks, reminders, recurring tasks, and other expanded limits. The current[Tweek pricing page](https://tweek.so/calendar/pricing) lists the plan comparison.


The limitation is documented scope: Tweek is aimed at visual simplicity rather than deep integrations or automatic scheduling. It will not solve a cross-tool consolidation problem or rebuild a crowded calendar automatically.


Tweek is best for a person or small group that already knows what belongs in the week and wants a clean place to see it. Choose another product when the hard part occurs before that point, such as collecting tasks from work systems, defining weekly objectives, or finding calendar capacity after meetings change.


A minimalist weekly board can improve honesty by limiting what fits on the screen. The user sees the commitments without layers of project metadata and can notice when one day becomes crowded. That constraint is useful for personal planning, study, household coordination, or a small shared routine. It becomes restrictive when work must be imported from several systems, assigned through complex projects, or rescheduled automatically. Tweek should therefore win on clarity and low maintenance, not be stretched into a role that requires the integrations and execution controls of a professional planning platform.


> **Tip** Plan one typical week, then add an urgent meeting midweek. Watch what loses capacity, where unfinished work goes, and whether the original priorities remain visible before committing to an annual plan.


## Which weekly planner app should you choose?


Choose Akiflow for a complete manual loop from task intake and goals to calendar time and review. Choose Sunsama for weekly objectives and reflection, Motion for automatic placement, Todoist for a lighter task-first week, and Tweek for a paper-like visual board. The correct planning model depends on which weekly decision currently fails.


Test the app with one real week, then introduce a midweek disruption: add an urgent meeting, move a deadline, and leave one task unfinished. Inspect whether lost capacity becomes visible, what happens to the displaced task, and whether the original priority survives. A planner that only works before the calendar changes is not managing the full week.


Separate review from scheduling when comparing products. Sunsama treats objectives as the weekly layer and leaves detailed timing to daily planning. Akiflow brings broader time frames and time blocking into the ritual. Motion uses task inputs to automate placement. Todoist and Tweek can support a user-created review, but the method itself remains more manual and self-defined.


Our overall recommendation is Akiflow for busy professionals because the same product handles connected task intake, weekly goals, broader time frames, calendar placement, and daily follow-through. The recommendation should yield to Motion when automation is non-negotiable, Sunsama when objective reflection is the desired habit, or a simpler product when the week does not require integrations or calendar depth.


A good evaluation ends with a short review after Friday, not immediately after setup. Count how many planned outcomes finished, how much work was displaced, and whether the planner explains what should happen next. Also note whether important tasks received calendar capacity before urgent meetings consumed the week. Akiflow offers the broadest manual planning loop in this group, but that breadth only matters when the user wants to review and place work deliberately. The other products earn their place by reducing ritual, increasing automation, lowering cost, or simplifying the visible week.


## Frequently asked questions


### What makes a weekly planner different from a task manager?


A weekly planner adds decisions about outcomes, calendar capacity, timing, and review to the task list. A task manager can still support a weekly routine, but the routine may need to be created by the user. Akiflow and Sunsama document weekly rituals; Motion automates placement; Todoist and Tweek provide task or visual structures that can support a self-directed review.


### Is Akiflow or Sunsama better for weekly planning?


Akiflow is better when weekly planning must include connected task intake, broader time frames, and calendar time blocking. Sunsama is better when the desired habit is setting and reflecting on weekly objectives while leaving detailed scheduling to the daily routine. Both are paid products with trials; the choice is between a fuller execution loop and a more objective-centered planning ritual.


### Does Motion plan the week automatically?


Yes. Motion places tasks around fixed calendar events using duration, priority, deadline, and availability. That can reduce manual placement, but the algorithm has more control over timing and sequence. The listed rate is $19 per seat each month with annual billing. It is best for someone who values automatic adjustment more than arranging every calendar block personally.


### Can Todoist work as a weekly planner?


Yes. Todoist can support a weekly routine through projects, filters, deadlines, reminders, and Pro features such as calendar layout and task duration. The official material reviewed does not document a dedicated weekly ritual, so the user must define the review and carry-forward method. It is a good fit when a task-first system is enough and prescribed planning steps are unnecessary.


### Who is Tweek best for?


Tweek is best for people who want a simple, paper-like weekly board with color coding, notes, sharing, and web or mobile access. The free plan can be used indefinitely; Premium is $5.99 monthly or $49.99 yearly and adds calendar sync, subtasks, reminders, and recurring tasks. Choose it when visual clarity and manual control matter more than cross-tool intake or automatic replanning.
